vignette:
He is 72 now, a soft-spoken software engineer who has spent most of his adult life in front of glowing screens, solving problems by reducing them to logic. When he speaks about the worst period of his life, though, logic falls away. He tells it in fragments at first, as if the story still lives in separate sealed compartments inside him.

As a young man, he travels abroad for contract work during a period of political unrest. He is good with machines and systems, the sort of person employers trust to keep complex operations running. He expects inconvenience, not danger. One evening he is taken by security forces after being mistaken for someone connected to dissidents. He remembers the suddenness of it most clearly: a hand at his shoulder, questions barked in a language he only partly understands, the blindfold tied too tightly around his eyes. After that come days he cannot fully count. In a concrete room, men interrogate him, accuse him, strike him when his answers do not satisfy them. He is deprived of sleep, forced to stand for long periods, threatened repeatedly, and made to believe he will not leave alive. He learns to listen for footsteps in the hall and to brace his body before the door opens. By the time he is released without explanation, his sense of time, trust, and bodily safety has been altered.

He returns to North America carrying one small bag and a silence he keeps for years. Friends tell him how lucky he is to be home. He nods and lets them believe that home has solved it. Instead, he finds that ordinary life has become unpredictable in ways he cannot explain. At night he startles awake drenched in sweat, certain for several seconds that he is back in the cell. He avoids sleeping deeply because the dreams are so vivid: the scrape of a chair, the smell of damp concrete, the feeling of not knowing when the next blow will come. He keeps a light on in the apartment and chooses places to live where he can control the locks, the windows, the sightlines to the door.

Work becomes both refuge and hiding place. Software engineering suits him because computers behave according to rules, and because long hours at a terminal give him a reason not to be with people. He gains a reputation for precision and reliability. Colleagues know him as the older engineer who catches subtle errors in code and prefers email to meetings. They do not see how hard he works to keep himself steady. If someone approaches his desk from behind, his whole body jerks before he can stop it. Raised voices in the office cafeteria make his heart pound. When a manager once shuts the conference room door during a tense discussion, he feels trapped so suddenly that he has to excuse himself and stand in the stairwell until the shaking in his hands subsides.

Over time he narrows his life. He never marries, though he speaks wistfully of two relationships that ended when the women told him he was emotionally elsewhere. He says he can be attentive in practical ways-fixing a router, cooking dinner, remembering the details of a doctor's appointment-but disappears when intimacy asks for vulnerability. He hates being asked, "What happened to you over there?" and hates even more the look on people's faces when he says, "I'd rather not talk about it." He keeps conversations on safer ground: operating systems, network security, baseball, weather.

Even in retirement age, he continues consulting part-time because idleness leaves too much room for memory. He rises early, checks and rechecks the apartment lock, and sits at his workstation before dawn. On difficult days, a small trigger can pull him backward. The buzz of an intercom, the metallic slam of a service door, a news story about political prisoners-suddenly he is no longer an elderly man in a quiet building but a young man trying to predict pain. He knows where he is, yet his body does not. His jaw tightens, his shoulders lift, and he scans the room automatically for exits. He feels embarrassed by this, even angry with himself. He says, "It's been fifty years. You'd think the system would have reset by now."

What troubles him almost as much as fear is the way the experience has shaped his view of other people. He wants to believe in decency, and often does in the abstract, but in close quarters he remains watchful. He sits facing doors in restaurants. He notices uniforms before faces. He does not tolerate being touched unexpectedly. When sleep is bad, he becomes irritable and withdrawn, letting messages go unanswered for days. Then he feels ashamed of the isolation he has built and the life that has grown around it-competent, orderly, narrow.

In sessions, he speaks more plainly than he expected to. He is not dramatic. He does not tell the story to seek pity. He tells it like an engineer tracing a fault through a system that once failed catastrophically and never fully recovered. Yet beneath his restraint is a man who has spent decades living as if danger might return without warning, and who still measures each ordinary day against the knowledge that, once, other human beings took away his control and taught his body not to forget.
